test.name: single_precision_compute
test.description: Peak arithmetic speed of the GPU's shader cores on 32-bit fractional numbers -- the ordinary float type. Nothing touches memory, so only the arithmetic units limit the rate.

test.name: half_precision_compute
test.description: Peak arithmetic speed on 16-bit fractional numbers -- half the size of a normal float, and what graphics and on-device AI mostly run on. NVIDIA shader cores reach full speed only on the packed form that does two at a time.

metric.name: half
metric.info: One value per thread at a time -- the plain, unvectorised case.

metric.name: half2
metric.info: Two values per thread at a time, packed into one instruction.

test.name: double_precision_compute
test.description: Peak arithmetic speed on 64-bit fractional numbers, the high-accuracy type scientific computing relies on. Consumer GeForce cards run these dozens of times slower than 32-bit; the datacenter parts do not.

test.name: mixed_precision_compute
test.description: Peak speed when the GPU multiplies 16-bit numbers but keeps the running total in 32 bits -- the accuracy-preserving pattern AI code uses. This is the shader cores, not the tensor cores.

test.name: bfloat16_compute
test.description: Peak speed on bfloat16 -- 16 bits arranged for AI work, trading digits of accuracy for the number range of a full float. Again the shader cores, with the tensor-core figure in the WMMA rows.

test.name: wmma_fp16
test.description: Peak speed of the tensor cores -- dedicated units that multiply whole 16x16 blocks of numbers in one step rather than one value at a time -- on 16-bit inputs with a 32-bit running total. This is the everyday precision of AI work.

test.name: wmma_fp16_f16
test.description: The same 16-bit tensor-core maths, but keeping the running total in 16 bits too. On GeForce cards the 32-bit-total form is deliberately capped at half rate, so this row is where the full tensor-core speed shows up.

test.name: wmma_bf16
test.description: Tensor cores on bfloat16 -- 16 bits arranged for AI work, trading digits of accuracy for the number range of a full float, which makes training far more forgiving.

test.name: wmma_tf32
test.description: Tensor cores on tf32, NVIDIA's trimmed-down stand-in for 32-bit float: it keeps the full number range but drops accuracy to fit the tensor cores.

test.name: wmma_fp64
test.description: Tensor cores on full 64-bit numbers, for scientific computing. Only the datacenter parts carry this hardware.

test.name: wmma_fp8_e4m3
test.description: Tensor cores on 8-bit numbers, in the variant that spends its bits on accuracy rather than range. Half the data of 16-bit per value, so it runs at roughly twice the rate.

test.name: wmma_fp8_e5m2
test.description: The same 8-bit tensor-core path in the other variant, which spends its bits on range rather than accuracy -- the one that copes with very large and very small values.

test.name: wmma_fp8_f16
test.description: The same 8-bit tensor-core maths, but keeping the running total in 16 bits rather than 32. On GeForce cards the 32-bit-total form is deliberately capped at half rate, so this row is where the full 8-bit speed shows up.

test.name: wmma_fp8_sparse
test.description: 8-bit numbers with structured sparsity: half the values in each group of four are known to be zero and are skipped, so the hardware does twice the useful work per step.

test.name: wmma_fp8_sparse_f16
test.description: 8-bit numbers with both tricks at once: half the values in each group of four are skipped as known zeros, and the running total is kept in 16 bits rather than 32. The fastest arrangement these tensor cores offer for 8-bit.

test.name: wmma_fp4_e2m1
test.description: Tensor cores on 4-bit numbers, the narrowest format the hardware handles. Blackwell and newer only.

test.name: wmma_mxf4_e2m1
test.description: 4-bit numbers with a shared scale factor per block of 32, the open MX format. The scale is what makes 4 bits usable for real models rather than a curiosity.

test.name: wmma_nvf4_e2m1
test.description: NVIDIA's own 4-bit block format, with a finer scale factor shared by every 16 values instead of every 32 -- more accurate than MX at the same width.

test.name: wmma_mxf4_sparse
test.description: The MX 4-bit path with structured sparsity: half the values in each group of four are known to be zero and are skipped, so the hardware does twice the useful work per step.

test.name: wmma_nvf4_sparse
test.description: NVIDIA's 4-bit block format with the same skip-the-zeros trick -- the fastest arrangement these tensor cores offer.

test.name: cublas-fp
test.description: Matrix-multiply speed through NVIDIA's own tuned library, on a large square problem. Where the WMMA rows show what the tensor cores can do in principle, this shows what shipping code reaches on the operation most AI work is built from.

metric.name: fp32
metric.info: Full 32-bit precision, on the ordinary shader cores rather than the tensor cores.

metric.name: fp64
metric.info: Full 64-bit precision, for scientific computing. Consumer cards run this far slower than the datacenter parts.

metric.name: tf32
metric.info: 32-bit numbers in and out, but rounded internally to a shorter form so the tensor cores can take them.

metric.name: fp16
metric.info: 16-bit inputs and totals -- the everyday precision of AI inference, and usually the fastest row here.

metric.name: bf16
metric.info: bfloat16 inputs with 32-bit totals -- 16 bits arranged for AI work, trading digits of accuracy for the number range of a full float.

metric.name: fp8_e4m3
metric.info: 8-bit inputs, in the variant that spends its bits on accuracy rather than range.

metric.name: fp8_e5m2
metric.info: 8-bit inputs including the variant that spends its bits on range rather than accuracy -- the usual choice for inference.

metric.name: mxf4_e2m1
metric.info: 4-bit inputs with a shared scale factor per block of 32, the open MX format. The scale is what makes 4 bits usable for real models.

metric.name: nvf4_e2m1
metric.info: NVIDIA's own 4-bit block format, with a finer scale shared by every 16 values instead of every 32 -- more accurate than MX at the same width.

test.name: integer_compute
test.description: Peak speed on 32-bit whole numbers -- the arithmetic behind indexing, addressing and bit manipulation, which shaders do alongside their fractional maths.

test.name: integer_compute_int8_dp
test.description: Peak speed of the 8-bit dot-product instruction, which multiplies four pairs of small whole numbers and sums them in one step -- the shader-core path for quantized (compressed) neural networks.

metric.name: int8_dp
metric.info: One chain of dot products, each waiting on the one before it.

metric.name: int8_dp2
metric.info: Two independent chains, so the GPU has a second dot product to get on with while the first is still finishing.

metric.name: int8_dp4
metric.info: Four independent chains.

metric.name: int8_dp8
metric.info: Eight independent chains. Where this stops improving on four, the hardware itself is the limit, not the waiting.

test.name: wmma_int8
test.description: Tensor cores on 8-bit whole numbers with a 32-bit running total -- the format quantized neural networks use when they are squeezed down to run fast on cheaper hardware.

test.name: wmma_int8_k32
test.description: The same 8-bit whole-number maths on NVIDIA's own native tile shape rather than the portable one, which the hardware feeds more efficiently.

test.name: wmma_int8_sparse
test.description: 8-bit whole numbers with structured sparsity: half the values in each group of four are known to be zero and are skipped, so the hardware does twice the useful work per step.

test.name: wmma_int4
test.description: Tensor cores on 4-bit whole numbers. Turing through Ada only -- NVIDIA dropped the integer 4-bit path afterwards in favour of the 4-bit float formats above.

test.name: cublas-int
test.description: The same tuned-library matrix multiply on whole-number formats, which is how a quantized (compressed) model actually runs.

metric.name: int8
metric.info: 8-bit whole numbers with 32-bit totals -- the format quantized neural networks use.

metric.name: int4
metric.info: 4-bit whole numbers. The library may refuse this even where the hardware claims it.

test.name: global_memory_bandwidth
test.description: How many bytes per second the GPU can stream out of its own memory, reading a buffer far too large to cache. Each reading fetches a different number of values per instruction, since wider fetches usually pull more through before the memory system saturates.

metric.name: float
metric.info: One value per thread at a time -- the plain, unvectorised case.

metric.name: float2
metric.info: Two values per thread at a time, packed into one instruction.

metric.name: float4
metric.info: Four values per thread at a time, as one 4-wide vector.

test.name: local_memory_bandwidth
test.description: How many bytes per second the GPU moves through shared memory -- the small on-chip scratchpad a block of threads passes data through, which never goes out to the card's main memory.

metric.name: float
metric.info: One value per thread at a time -- the plain, unvectorised case.

metric.name: float2
metric.info: Two values per thread at a time, packed into one instruction.

metric.name: float4
metric.info: Four values per thread at a time, as one 4-wide vector.

test.name: image_memory_bandwidth
test.description: How many bytes per second the GPU reads through its texture units, which take a different path to memory than plain buffer reads. Each pixel of the image is read exactly once, so caching cannot flatter the number.

metric.name: float4
metric.info: Each fetch returns one whole pixel -- four 32-bit colour values, 16 bytes.

test.name: transfer_bandwidth
test.description: How fast data crosses between the computer's own memory and the card's, over the PCIe link. That link is far narrower than either side's own memory, which is what makes moving data to the GPU worth avoiding. Both readings use pinned host memory, the fast path.

metric.name: h2d_pinned
metric.info: Host to device: sending data up to the card.

metric.name: d2h_pinned
metric.info: Device to host: reading results back down. Often a little slower than the other direction.

test.name: kernel_launch_latency
test.description: The overhead of asking the GPU to do anything at all, measured with a kernel that does no work. It is what small, frequent GPU jobs pay before any of their own work begins.

metric.name: dispatch
metric.info: One way only: from the moment the host submits the work to the moment the GPU starts running it. CUDA exposes no clock the host and GPU share, so this is reported on the other backends but not here.
metric.reason: Not measurable via CUDA driver API

metric.name: roundtrip
metric.info: The full round trip -- submit, run, and hear back that it finished. This is what the host waits for if it has nothing else to get on with.
